title: The Anatomy of a Quad: Every Part & the Block Diagram
html:
The ten subsystems

An FPV quad looks like a tangle of wires, but it is really ten well-defined subsystems. Once you can name each one and trace where its power and signal come from, every build, repair, and bug becomes tractable. Here is the full cast:

SubsystemJobTalks to
Battery (LiPo/Li-ion)Stores energy, supplies main power busESC / PDB via XT60/XT30
ESC (4-in-1 or 4× single)Switches battery DC into 3-phase to spin motorsFC (signal), motors (3 wires each)
Brushless motors ×4Convert electrical power to thrustESC only
Flight controller (FC)The brain: reads gyro, runs PID loop, commands ESCEverything
Radio receiver (RX)Receives stick commands from your transmitterFC UART
FPV cameraCaptures the live imageVTX (analog) or FC/air-unit (digital)
Video transmitter (VTX)Beams video to your gogglesCamera + FC + antenna
GPS/compass (optional)Position, rescue, return-to-homeFC UART + I2C
PDB / power filteringDistributes and cleans powerBattery → everything
AntennasRadiate RF for control link and videoRX / VTX

Two networks: power and signal

Keep these mentally separate. Power flows from the battery to the ESC, which feeds motors directly and steps voltage down (via a BEC/regulator on the FC or ESC) to 5V/9V/10V rails for the FC, RX, camera, and VTX. Signal is the low-current wiring: the FC sends throttle commands to each ESC over a single wire (DShot), the RX feeds stick data to a FC UART, and the GPS streams NMEA-style data over another UART plus magnetometer data over I2C.

The block diagram

quad-block-diagram
[ LiPo ]--XT60--+ | VBAT (raw 14.8-25.2V) +------+------+ | 4-in-1 ESC |---3ph---> Motor M1 | (BLHeli_32) |---3ph---> Motor M2 | |---3ph---> Motor M3 | |---3ph---> Motor M4 +--+--------+--+ DShot | | VBAT+5V (BEC) v v +-----------+ UART1 +--------+ | FC |<--------->| RX |~)) control link | (gyro+MCU)| UART2 +--------+ | |<--------->| VTX |~)) 5.8GHz video | | UART3 ^ | |<----------+ | video in | | GPS+I2C | | +-----------+ [ FPV CAM ]--+ ^ | UART4 [ GPS / compass ]
Mental model.
The FC is a hub. Almost every smart peripheral connects to it on a dedicated UART (a TX/RX wire pair) plus a power and ground wire. Master "which UART does what" and configuration stops being mysterious.
Props off.
Any time you power a quad on the bench to configure it, remove the propellers first. A quad that arms unexpectedly with props on can cause serious lacerations.
▸Hands-On

Draw a complete quad block diagram from memory.

  1. On paper, place the battery at the top and motors at the bottom.
  2. Draw the ESC and FC between them; route VBAT power lines as thick arrows.
  3. Add RX, camera, VTX, and GPS, connecting each to an FC UART with a thin signal line.
  4. Label every line as either POWER (with voltage) or SIGNAL (with protocol: DShot, UART, I2C).
  5. Verify every peripheral has power, ground, and a data path back to the FC.

title: The Frame: Sizes, Materials & Geometry
html:
Why the frame defines the build

The frame is the skeleton that dictates which propellers fit, which motors bolt on, and how much abuse the quad survives. Frame size is named by the largest prop it can swing, measured diagonally between motor centers for the wheelbase. Pick the frame first; nearly every other component flows from that choice.

Common sizes

ClassPropWheelbaseTypical motorAUWUse
Tiny whoop31-40mm65-75mm0802-110220-35gIndoor, beginner
Toothpick / 3"3"120-140mm1404-1507120-250gLight freestyle, sub-250
5" standard5"210-230mm2207/2306400-700gFreestyle, racing, the do-everything class
7" long range7"290-320mm2806.5-2807500-900gCruising, distance, cinematic

Materials

Carbon fiber (3K weave) is the standard for arms and the main plate: extremely stiff, light, and strong. Arm thickness matters most — a 5" freestyle frame uses 4mm arms for durability; racers drop to 3mm to save weight. Watch two carbon hazards: it is electrically conductive (a frayed strand can short a pad) and the dust is a respiratory and eye irritant when cutting or sanding.

Injection-molded plastic / TPU dominates whoops and ducts because it flexes instead of snapping, and the prop ducts protect both the props and bystanders. TPU is also the go-to 3D-printing material for antenna mounts, camera cages, and bumpers because it absorbs impact.

Geometry that matters

  • True-X vs stretched-X: True-X spaces all four motors equally (balanced freestyle); stretched-X moves rear motors back for high-speed stability (racing).
  • Arm replaceability: bolt-on individual arms let you swap one cracked arm instead of the whole frame — a huge maintenance win.
  • Standoff height: the gap between the bottom and top plate must clear your stacked FC/ESC plus capacitor.
  • Camera cage width: 19mm (micro), 21mm (nano), or 14mm — must match your camera.
Mounting standard.
Most 5" stacks use the 30.5×30.5mm bolt pattern with M3 hardware; micro stacks use 20×20mm with M2. Confirm your frame's mounting holes match your electronics before buying.
Inspect after crashes.
A hairline crack in a carbon arm can let go mid-flight and throw a prop. Flex each arm and check around motor screw holes after any hard impact; retire cracked arms.
▸Hands-On

Build a three-frame comparison sheet.

  1. Pick one whoop, one 3", and one 5" frame from a vendor site.
  2. Record prop size, wheelbase (mm), arm thickness (mm), weight (g), and mounting pattern.
  3. Note geometry: true-X or stretched-X, and whether arms are replaceable.
  4. Write one sentence per frame on the mission it suits best.

title: Brushless Motors: Stator Size, KV & Thrust
html:
Reading the number

A motor labeled 2207 1900KV packs two key specs. The four digits are the stator dimensions in millimeters: 22 = stator diameter, 07 = stator height. A bigger stator (more iron and copper) makes more torque and handles more heat, at the cost of weight. KV is rpm per volt with no load — it sets the speed/torque trade-off.

StatorClassTypical KVBattery
0802-1103Whoop11000-190001S
1404-15073" / toothpick2800-45003S-4S
2207 / 23065"1700-2000 (6S), 2400-2750 (4S)4S-6S
2806.5-28077" long range1200-15006S

KV and voltage are a pair

Higher KV spins faster per volt but produces less torque and draws more current, demanding a smaller/lighter prop. The industry shifted from 4S to 6S precisely to lower KV: at 6S you use a ~1900KV motor instead of a ~2750KV 4S motor, achieving the same prop speed at half the current. Lower current means thinner wires, less heat, and less voltage sag. Rule of thumb: roughly match KV to voltage so KV × cells × 3.7 ≈ 40,000-50,000 for a 5".

Reading a thrust table

Manufacturers publish bench data per prop and voltage. The columns that matter:

  • Thrust (g): at full throttle. You want a total (4 motors) thrust-to-weight ratio of at least 4:1 for freestyle, 8:1+ for racing.
  • Current (A): peak draw per motor — sizes your ESC and battery C-rating.
  • Efficiency (g/W): grams of thrust per watt. Higher is better. This is where long-range builds optimize.
  • Temperature: if the table notes the motor ran hot, that combo is over-propped.
thrust-table 2207 1700KV @ 6S (sample)
Prop Thr Amps g/W HQ 5.1x3.1 1850g 38.0A 5.1 (hot, over-propped) GF 5x4.3x3 1620g 30.5A 6.4 (efficient sweet spot) HQ 5x3.5x3 1430g 24.0A 6.2
Efficiency hunting.
The best thrust-to-current combo is rarely the highest-thrust row. Scan the g/W column for the peak, then confirm the current stays within your ESC and battery limits. That is your hover-friendly, long-flight setup.
Heat kills.
A motor too hot to hold for 2 seconds after a flight is being overworked — usually too much prop or KV. Sustained over-temp demagnetizes the magnets and burns windings. Drop pitch or prop size.
▸Hands-On

Find the efficiency sweet spot for one motor.

  1. Open a manufacturer thrust table for a 5" motor at your target voltage.
  2. Add or read a g/W (efficiency) column for each prop row.
  3. Identify the prop with the highest g/W where current stays under your ESC rating.
  4. Compute total thrust ×4 and divide by a 600g AUW to get thrust-to-weight.

title: ESCs: Single vs 4-in-1, Amp Ratings & BLHeli
html:
What an ESC does

The Electronic Speed Controller takes the FC's throttle command and the battery's DC voltage and switches it into the precisely-timed three-phase AC that spins a brushless motor. It also reads back rotor position (sensorless, via back-EMF) thousands of times per second. Modern ESCs run digital protocols — DShot600 is the standard for 5" builds — which are noise-immune and let the FC and ESC exchange telemetry and bidirectional rpm for RPM-filtering.

Single vs 4-in-1

4× single ESC4-in-1 ESC
LayoutOne ESC per armOne board under the FC
WiringSolder battery + signal ×4One battery pad, ribbon to FC
RepairSwap one bad ESCReplace whole board
Weight/clean buildHeavier, messierLighter, tidy stack
Use7"+ where high amps need spread heatDominant on 3"-5"

4-in-1 boards dominate because they fold the entire power section into one stack layer with a single battery solder joint and a clean ribbon cable to the FC. They also integrate the capacitor pad and current sensor.

Sizing the amp rating

The headline number (e.g. 45A, 60A) is the continuous rating per motor. The rule: ESC continuous rating should comfortably exceed your motor's peak current from the thrust table, with margin. If a motor peaks at 38A on your chosen prop, a 45A ESC leaves only 18% headroom — fine for freestyle, tight for racing. A 60A ESC gives ~58% headroom and runs cooler.

esc-sizing
motor peak (1 motor) = 38A choose ESC continuous = 45A (headroom 18%, ok freestyle) = 60A (headroom 58%, racing/punch) 4-in-1 "4x60A" means 60A PER motor, not total.
Burst vs continuous.
Ignore the big "burst" amp number on the box; it is only valid for a few seconds. Size to the continuous rating. Also check the voltage rating: a 3-6S ESC is safe to 25.2V; never feed a 6S pack into a 4S-only ESC.

BLHeli firmware

ESC firmware is configured in BLHeli_S, Bluejay (open-source upgrade for BLHeli_S 8-bit hardware, adds DShot300/600 and bidirectional rpm), or BLHeli_32 / AM32 (32-bit, full telemetry). Key settings: motor timing, motor direction (reverse a spinning-wrong motor in software, not by re-soldering), and enabling bidirectional DShot for RPM filtering.

Bench safely.
Always set motor direction and run motor tests with props removed. In Betaflight's Motors tab, the spin-test checkbox is a real liability with blades attached.
▸Hands-On

Size a 4-in-1 ESC for a given motor.

  1. Read your motor's peak current from its thrust table at your voltage and prop.
  2. Multiply by ~1.3-1.5 to set a minimum continuous ESC rating.
  3. Pick a 4-in-1 ESC whose per-motor rating and voltage class (e.g. 3-6S) cover it.
  4. Write one sentence justifying the headroom for your flying style.

title: The Flight Controller: MCU, Gyro/IMU & UARTs
html:
The brain

The flight controller runs the firmware (Betaflight, on most FPV quads) that reads the gyro 8,000 times a second, runs the PID loop, mixes the result, and sends a throttle value to each ESC. Three spec lines decide whether an FC is good enough: the MCU, the gyro/IMU, and the UART count.

MCU generation

MCUClassNotes
F4 (STM32F405)BudgetCapable, but limited UARTs and can't run highest gyro loop rates
F7MidMore UARTs, better peripheral handling
H7 (STM32H743)Modern standard480MHz, 8kHz loop easily, plenty of UARTs, headroom for filtering

For a new 5" build, an H7 (or a clean F7) is the safe choice. F4 is fine for budget and micro builds.

Gyro / IMU

The gyro measures rotation rate; the accelerometer (together they form the IMU) measures gravity for self-leveling modes. Quality matters because gyro noise forces heavier filtering, which adds latency. Common parts: the older MPU6000 (SPI, very clean, beloved), and newer ICM-42688-P and BMI270 (the BMI270 is the modern default after MPU6000 went scarce). Confirm the gyro is on the SPI bus, not I2C — SPI supports the fast sample rates FPV needs.

UARTs: count them before you buy

A UART is a hardware serial port (a TX and RX pad pair). Every smart peripheral wants one. Tally your peripherals against available UARTs before buying:

uart-plan (H7 FC, 6 UARTs)
UART1 -> ELRS receiver (Serial RX) UART2 -> digital VTX / air unit (MSP+OSD) UART3 -> GPS module (NMEA/UBX) UART4 -> smartaudio (analog VTX control) UART5 -> ESC telemetry UART6 -> spare I2C -> compass (magnetometer) SoftSerial -> backup if you run out

Other pads to check: a dedicated RX/SBUS pad, 5V and 9V/10V regulated outputs (the VTX often wants 9V), a cam pad with on-screen-display passthrough, an onboard OSD chip (AT7456 for analog), a barometer, blackbox flash for logging, and an LED pad.

SoftSerial is a fallback, not a plan.
Betaflight can emulate extra serial ports in software, but they are slower and use CPU. If your peripheral list needs five UARTs, buy a board with five real ones rather than relying on SoftSerial.
Check the BEC current.
The FC's 5V/9V regulators have current limits (often ~2-3A). A power-hungry digital VTX plus camera plus GPS can exceed a weak 5V BEC and brown out the FC mid-flight. Read the regulator rating on the spec page.
▸Hands-On

Map a real FC's ports to a peripheral plan.

  1. Open a real H7 or F7 FC product page and list its UARTs, regulated outputs, and pads.
  2. List your peripherals: RX, VTX, GPS, ESC telemetry, camera control.
  3. Assign each peripheral to a specific UART or pad in a table.
  4. Confirm the 9V output exists if your VTX needs it, and the 5V BEC current covers your loads.

title: Propellers: Size, Pitch & Blade Count
html:
Decoding a prop code

A prop labeled 5x4.3x3 reads as diameter × pitch × blade count: 5-inch diameter, 4.3-inch pitch, 3 blades. Some props add an extra digit (e.g. 51466 = 5.1" dia, 4.6" pitch, 6... no — 51466 means 5.1 diameter, 4.6 pitch, with the trailing digits being a model code). Stick to the explicit D x P x B form and you'll never be confused.

FieldMeansMore of it →
DiameterTip-to-tip inchesMore thrust + grip, more current, set by frame
PitchInches it would travel per rotation in solid materialMore top speed, more current, less low-end grip
Blade count2, 3, or moreMore grip + control, less efficiency, more drag

Pitch is your gearing

Think of pitch like a transmission. Low pitch (e.g. 3.5) is a low gear: snappy response, strong low-end grip, runs cooler, great for technical freestyle and proximity. High pitch (e.g. 4.9+) is overdrive: higher top speed and a longer punch, but it draws more amps, runs hotter, and feels less precise at part throttle.

Blade count

  • 2-blade (bi-blade): most efficient, fastest, least drag — racing and speed runs. Less grip, can feel loose.
  • 3-blade (tri-blade): the universal freestyle choice. Excellent control and grip, smoother, slightly less efficient. The default.
  • 4+ blade: maximum grip and locked-in feel for tight cinematic work or ducted whoops, at a real efficiency and current cost.
prop-pick by mission
Racing -> 5x4.8x2 (low drag, top speed, efficient) Freestyle -> 5x4.3x3 (grip + control, all-round) Cruise/LR -> 7x4x3 (big dia, low pitch, high g/W) Cinematic -> 5x4.3x4 (locked-in, draggy)

Practical notes

Props are directional and come as CW/CCW sets — Betaflight's default "props-out" config spins front motors outward. The number molded near the hub or the leading-edge shape tells direction. Material is usually polycarbonate; cheap props flex and lose efficiency, while a quality prop holds its shape under load. Balance matters less than it used to, but a chipped or cracked prop must be retired immediately — it causes vibration that the gyro picks up as noise and can shatter at full throttle.

Props are blades.
A 5" tri-blade at full throttle spins fast enough to cut to the bone. Never spin a quad with props on near people or your face. Inspect every prop before flight; replace any with chips, cracks, or a bent hub. Treat a quad with props on as armed.
One variable at a time.
When tuning prop choice, change only pitch OR blade count between packs so you can feel what each does. Log motor temps after each flight to catch an over-propped setup.
▸Hands-On

Compare three props and assign each a mission.

  1. Pick three 5" props differing in pitch and blade count (e.g. 5x4.8x2, 5x4.3x3, 5x4.3x4).
  2. For each, predict top speed, low-end grip, efficiency, and current draw.
  3. Assign one to racing, one to freestyle, one to efficient cruising.
  4. Write the one-sentence reason for each choice.

title: LiPo & Li-ion: S-Count, mAh, C-Rating & Connectors
html:
Decoding a label

A pack marked 6S 1300mAh 100C tells you everything you need. Read it field by field:

SpecMeans
6S6 cells in series. LiPo nominal 3.7V/cell → 22.2V nominal, 25.2V at full charge (4.2V/cell)
1300mAhCapacity: 1.3 amp-hours of charge stored
100CDischarge rate: max continuous current = C × capacity = 100 × 1.3A = 130A

The S-count (in series) sets voltage; a P-count (in parallel, common in Li-ion packs like 4S2P) multiplies capacity. Full and empty voltages: LiPo charges to 4.2V/cell, you land at ~3.5V/cell under load, and you never store at full.

C-rating and real current

C-rating times capacity gives the claimed max continuous current. Honest LiPos: a true 100C 1300mAh delivers 130A continuous — comfortably above a 5" quad's ~120A peak (4 motors × ~30A). Manufacturers exaggerate C-ratings, so judge a pack by how little voltage it sags under a punch, not the printed number. Sag below 3.3V/cell under load means the pack can't keep up.

LiPo vs Li-ion

LiPoLi-ion (e.g. 18650, 21700)
Energy densityLowerHigher (much more Wh per gram)
Discharge rateVery high (50-150C)Low (~10-35A/cell)
Best forRacing, freestyle, punchLong range / endurance cruising
Flight time3-5 min20-40+ min on a 7"

Choose LiPo when you need raw power and burst current. Choose Li-ion for a 7" long-range rig flown at gentle throttle, where energy density buys huge flight times — but never punch a Li-ion pack hard; it sags badly and overheats.

Connectors

  • XT60: standard for 5"/6"/7" packs, handles the full current.
  • XT30: lighter, for 3" / toothpick (sub-~30A).
  • BT2.0 / PH2.0 / GNB27: whoop and 1S micro packs.
  • Balance lead (JST-XH): the extra connector that lets the charger balance each cell — always charge balanced.
LiPo safety — non-negotiable.
Charge on a fireproof surface and never unattended. Store at 3.8V/cell (storage charge), not full. Never over-discharge below 3.0V/cell. Never puncture, crush, or fly a puffed pack — a swollen cell is failing and must be retired and disposed of properly (discharge to 0V in salt water, then recycle). A LiPo fire is violent and self-sustaining.
Set a sane low-voltage alarm.
A buzzer or OSD warning at 3.5V/cell under load tells you to land. Repeatedly draining packs flat destroys their C-rating and lifespan.
▸Hands-On

Decode three real battery labels.

  1. Find three packs: e.g. 6S 1300mAh 100C LiPo, 4S 1500mAh 75C LiPo, 4S2P Li-ion.
  2. For each, compute full voltage, nominal voltage, and max continuous current.
  3. State which suits a racing quad and which suits a long-range rig, and why.
  4. Confirm each pack's connector matches its intended quad class.

title: The Control & Video Chain: Receiver, FPV Camera, VTX & Antennas
html:
Two independent radio links

Every FPV quad runs two separate RF links: the control link (your sticks → receiver) and the video link (camera → VTX → goggles). They use different frequencies and must not be confused. Both need matched, well-mounted antennas to work at range.

The receiver (RX)

The receiver pairs ("binds") to your transmitter and feeds stick data to an FC UART, typically via the serial protocol. The modern standard is ExpressLRS (ELRS) at 2.4GHz or 915MHz — open-source, extremely long range, low latency. Older systems include Crossfire (TBS, 900MHz) and FrSky. Match the RX to your TX protocol: an ELRS RX needs an ELRS TX module. Wire it as 5V / GND / TX / RX to a spare UART and select the protocol in Betaflight's Receiver tab. The RX antenna should be mounted away from the VTX antenna and carbon, ideally pointing up.

Analog vs digital video

AnalogDigital (DJI / HDZero / Walksnail)
ImageLower res, gracefully degrades to staticSharp HD, breaks up suddenly at the edge
LatencyLowest (~ms)Low but higher than analog (HDZero is close)
Weight/costLight, cheapHeavier air unit, pricier
CameraSeparate analog cam + VTXOften an integrated camera + air-unit

The FPV camera

An analog camera (e.g. Caddx Ratel, Foxeer) outputs a composite video signal to the VTX and accepts 5V (check — some take up to a wider input). Specs to match: sensor (CMOS, low-light performance), aspect ratio (4:3 vs 16:9 — match your goggles), lens FOV (~160°), and physical size (micro 19mm, nano 14mm) to fit your frame's camera cage. The camera's control wire can route to a UART for on-screen menu access.

The VTX and antennas

The analog video transmitter takes the camera signal and broadcasts it on 5.8GHz. Key specs: power (25mW for racing/legal indoor, up to 600mW-1W+ for range — check your region's legal limit and licensing), band/channel (Raceband etc.), input voltage (many want 9V or take a wide 7-26V), and a control protocol (SmartAudio or Tramp) wired to a UART so you can change power/channel from your goggles. The VTX gets warm — it needs airflow and must never be powered without an antenna connected.

Never power a VTX without an antenna.
Transmitting with no antenna reflects RF power back into the amplifier and can burn it out in seconds. Connect the antenna before you ever plug in the battery.

Antennas: video uses circular-polarized antennas (RHCP standard) — a stubby "lollipop" or pagoda. Linear whips are for the control link. Match polarization between your VTX and goggle antennas, and keep antenna connectors (SMA/MMCX/U.FL) consistent.

Power limits are regulated.
Maximum legal VTX output power and the 5.8GHz channels you may use vary by country and may require an amateur radio license. Verify current local rules (FCC in the US, plus FAA registration for the aircraft) before transmitting at high power.
▸Hands-On

Spec a matched control + video chain.

  1. Choose analog or digital, then pick a matching RX, camera, VTX, and antenna set.
  2. Confirm the RX protocol matches your transmitter (e.g. ELRS to ELRS).
  3. Check input voltage for the camera and VTX against your FC's regulated outputs (5V, 9V).
  4. Verify antenna connectors (SMA/U.FL) and polarization match your goggles.

title: GPS/Compass, Power Distribution & Reading a Real Parts List
html:
GPS and compass: when you need them

Most 5" freestyle and racing quads fly without GPS. You add a GPS module when you want: GPS Rescue (return-to-home / failsafe recovery if you lose video or link), position telemetry, distance/home-arrow OSD, or autonomous-style features. It is close to mandatory on a 7" long-range build, where losing sight of the quad over distance is the norm.

The module contains a GNSS receiver (look for M10-generation chips like the u-blox M10, fast lock, many satellites) and often an integrated compass/magnetometer. The GPS streams position over a UART; the compass talks over I2C. For pure GPS Rescue in Betaflight you often don't strictly need the compass, and it must be mounted away from current-carrying wires and the VTX to avoid magnetic interference. Mount the GPS on a mast or the top plate with a clear sky view.

gps-wiring
GPS 5V -> FC 5V GPS GND -> FC GND GPS TX -> FC UARTn RX GPS RX -> FC UARTn TX MAG SDA -> FC I2C SDA (if compass used) MAG SCL -> FC I2C SCL

Power distribution

On modern builds the 4-in-1 ESC is the PDB — the battery solders to one pad on the ESC, which distributes power to the motors and provides a regulated 5V/sometimes 9V BEC to the stack. Standalone PDBs survive mainly on builds with four single ESCs (large quads). The other critical power part is the capacitor: a low-ESR electrolytic cap (e.g. 35V 470-1000µF) soldered across the battery pads to absorb voltage spikes from the ESC switching — it protects electronics and cleans up video noise. Always fit it.

Voltage rating the cap.
The cap's voltage rating must exceed the pack's full voltage with margin: for 6S (25.2V) use a 35V cap, never a 25V one. An under-rated cap can fail explosively.

Reading a real parts list

When you see a published build, sort every line into a category and then sanity-check compatibility:

  1. Frame — note prop size and mounting pattern (30.5×30.5?).
  2. Motors — stator + KV; does KV suit the battery cell count?
  3. ESC — continuous amps ≥ motor peak? Voltage class covers the pack?
  4. FC — enough UARTs for RX + VTX + GPS? 9V BEC if the VTX needs it?
  5. VTX + camera — input voltage available on the FC? Camera size fits the cage?
  6. RX — protocol matches the radio?
  7. Battery — S-count matches motors/ESC; C-rating covers peak current; XT60.
  8. Props — diameter matches the frame.
Register and verify rules.
In the US, drones over 250g must be registered with the FAA and many require Remote ID; flight is subject to airspace rules. Requirements differ by country and change — always verify current FAA/local regulations before flying.
Final pre-flight.
Props on last. Confirm failsafe (motors stop / GPS Rescue) is configured and tested on the bench before the first flight. A quad without a working failsafe is a flyaway waiting to happen.
▸Hands-On

Audit a real published 5" build parts list.

  1. Find a complete 5" build list online (frame, motors, ESC, FC, VTX, camera, RX, battery, props).
  2. Label each line item by category.
  3. Check the eight compatibility points above; write PASS or a concern for each.
  4. Flag any voltage, UART-count, or mounting mismatch you find.
